sections.heading: Energy harvesting from ambient low-frequency magnetic field using magneto-mechano-electric composite cantilever
sections.text:
Guoxi Liu, Penghong Ci, and Shuxiang Donga)   
Department of Materials Science and Engineering, College of Engineering, Peking University,   
Beijing 100871 , People's Republic of China

(Received 12 December 2013; accepted 2 January 2014; published online 24 January 2014)

A magneto-mechano-electric (MME) composite cantilever for energy harvesting from ambient low-frequency magnetic field has been investigated in this study. The MME composite cantilever is made of a piezoelectric bimorph with NdFeB magnets attached at its tip. The properties of the MME composite cantilever based energy harvester were theoretically predicted by using the equivalent circuit model. The experimental results show that the maximum power density for excitations at the short- and open-circuit resonance frequencies $( < 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z } )$ is $1 \mathrm { { 1 } } . 7 3 \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { O e } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { { c m } } ^ { 3 }$ , which is one order of magnitude higher than that of previously reported magnetoelectric energy harvester. The research has proved the potential application of the composite cantilever for harvesting ambient low-frequency magnetic field energy. $©$ 2014 AIP Publishing LLC. [http://dx.doi.org/10.1063/1.4862876]

Energy harvesting technologies from ambient lowfrequency vibration based on piezoelectric, electrostatic, and electromagnetic transduction mechanisms for running wireless sensors and low-powered electronics have drawn growing attention over the last decade.1-8 Like low level environmental vibration, stray low-frequency magnetic field $( < 1 0 0 \ : \mathrm { H z } )$ exists extensively, such as electromagnetic noises produced by power-supply systems and periodic geomagnetic anomalies due to vehicles' disturbance, which can also be considered as an attractive energy source. However, there are few focus and researches on low-frequency magnetic energy harvesting. In low-frequency range, especially at low-frequency below $5 0 \mathrm { H z }$ , traditional magnetic energy harvesting technology based on Faraday's induction law is not effective any more.9,10 Additionally, the limited number and volume of turns that can be achieved by using coils are some of the main practical limitations. Recently, magnetoelectric (ME) composites of magnetostrictive and piezoelectric phases, in which the electric and magnetic behaviors are coupled elastically with each other, have lead a way for lowfrequency magnetic energy harvesting. Dong et al.11 reported bi-mechanism of the bulk type ME composites for harvesting both mechanical vibration and magnetic field energy, showing the rationality and feasibility of ME comtheoretically analyzed the performances of various ME composite structures, providing an optimal way for the design of ME energy harvesters. And Onuta et al.15 experimentally confirmed that thin-film ME laminated composites based energy harvester had a considerably high power density.

R, Xi  l d Lu  .v oos a different type of magneto-mechano-electric (MME) composite structure, which is constructed by a cantilever consisting of a piezoelectric bimorph (or piezoelectric composite beam) and tip magnets without magnetostrictive phase, and its ME coupling is based on magnetic force moment effect and piezoelectric effect. This MME composite structure possesses colossal low-frequency ME coupling and brings about a remarkable enhancement in ME coefficients in lowfrequency range. Thereupon, it suggests that this MME composite structure has a strong capability of energy conversion between magnetic and electric fields in low-frequency range and thus can be considered as an alternative design for lowfrequency magnetic energy harvesting. The purpose of this Letter is to investigate the energy harvesting performance of such a MME composite cantilever.

The piezoelectric bimorph/tip magnets MME composite cantilever is schematically illustrated in Fig. 1. The piezoelectric bimorph was made of a brass sheet $( 6 0 \mu \mathrm { m }$ in thickness) sandwiched by a pair of identical piezoelectric twin plates (piezoceramics $\mathrm { P b } ( \mathrm { Z r } , \mathrm { T i } ) { \mathrm { O } } _ { 3 }$ (PZT-5H)) poled in thickness (denoted by $P$ ), which was bonded by epoxy resin (West system 206/105, USA) and cured for more than $2 4 \mathrm { ~ h ~ }$ at room temperature. And the piezoelectric bimorph was electrically connected in parallel and mechanically clamped at one end. Each plate of the piezoelectric bimorph was chosen to be $3 5 \mathrm { m m } \ \mathrm { ( l e n g t h ) } \times 7 \mathrm { m m } \ \mathrm { ( w i d t h ) } \times 0 . 5 \mathrm { m m }$ (thickness) in size, which is in accordance with the size of typical wireless sensor nodes.20 The material parameters of the used PZT-5H were obtained by a precision impedance analyzer (Agilent 4294A, USA) using resonance-antiresonance method.21 Two commercially supplied NdFeB magnets (the volume $V _ { m } = 0 . 5 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ for each, the mass density $\rho _ { m } = 7 . 4 \mathrm { g } / \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 } )$ whose magnetization direction is denoted by $J$ were attached at the free end of the piezoelectric bimorph by magnetic attraction of themselves. The remnant magnetic polarization of the used NdFeB magnets is $J _ { r } = 1 . 2 \mathrm { T }$ Under an ambient AC magnetic field $H _ { a c }$ along the longitudinal direction of the MME composite cantilever, the tip magnets will generate a magnetic force moment $M = 2 V _ { m } J _ { r } H _ { a c }$ applied to the piezoelectric bimorph, resulting in a bending vibration of the MME composite cantilever. In this process, the ambient magnetic energy is transferred into the mechanical energy of the MME composite cantilever. Subsequently, the piezoelectric bimorph converts the acquired mechanical energy into the electric power output through a load resistance $R _ { L }$ via piezoelectric effect. That is how the piezoelectric bimorph/tip magnets MME composite cantilever implements magnetic energy harvesting.

![](images/8b9c9aee781f47d471bb3a9dd2937219d09449927430311620eb31e4df6c77ca.jpg)  
FIG. 1. (a) Schematic illustration of the piezoelectric bimorph/tip magnets MME composite cantilever; (b) the experimental setup for the MME composite cantilever.

The impedance spectrum of the MME composite cantilever was acquired from the precision impedance analyzer (Agilent 4294A, USA). In our measurements, the ambient AC magnetic field $H _ { a c }$ was generated by a pair of Helmholtz coils $\mathrm { 8 0 m m }$ in diameter) powered by a signal generator (Agilent 33522A, USA) and the amplitude of $H _ { a c }$ was maintained at $1 \mathrm { O e }$ .The tip magnets were located in the center of the pair of Helmholtz coils during measurements (see Fig. 1(b)). The induced voltage output $V _ { o }$ (peak value) across $R _ { L }$ was directly measured by either an oscilloscope (Agilent 6014A, USA) for large signal $\mathrm { \Gamma ( > 1 0 0 m V ) }$ or by a lock-in amplifier (Stanford Research 850, USA) for small signal $\left( < 1 0 0 \mathrm { m V } \right)$ . And the generated electric power output $P _ { o }$ across $R _ { L }$ was calculated from $P _ { o } = V _ { o } ^ { 2 } / 2 R _ { L }$ .The induced charge output $Q _ { e }$ (peak value) under short-circuit condition was monitored by a charge meter (Kistler 5015A, Switzerland) connected to the oscilloscope. All measurements were conducted at room temperature.

The magneto-mechano-electric equivalent circuit approach, which was first proposed by Dong et al.,2,23 is a useful tool for analyzing the dynamic behaviors of ME sensors, transformers, and energy harvesters, especially at resonance. And Ha et al.24,25 gave the equivalent circuit models for piezoelectric bimorph. Accordingly, we can draw up a modified resonant equivalent circuit model for the MME composite cantilever with a load resistance (see Fig. 2(a)). Figure 2(b) illustrates the simplified equivalent circuit without excitation (with the input terminal shorted)26 and the inclusive components can be determined by the measured impedance spectrum as shown in Fig. 2(c). Correspondingly, $V _ { o }$ across $R _ { L }$ can be given as

$$
V _ { o } = \bigg | \frac { \varphi _ { p } R _ { L } } { Z _ { m } ( 1 + j \omega C _ { 0 } R _ { L } ) + \varphi _ { p } ^ { 2 } R _ { L } } M \bigg | ,
$$

where the mechanical impedance Zm = jωLm +Rm + m and $\omega$ is the angular frequency of the applied magnetic field. For open-circuit (oc) condition $( R _ { L }  \infty$ ), $V _ { o }$ becomes

$$
V _ { o } ^ { o c } = \bigg | \frac { \varphi _ { p } } { j \omega C _ { 0 } Z _ { m } + \varphi _ { p } ^ { 2 } } M \bigg | .
$$

Whereas for short-circuit (sc) condition $( R _ { L } = 0$ , the induced charge output $Q _ { e }$ is preferred to be chosen as the measured signal and can be expressed as

$$
Q _ { e } ^ { s c } = \left| \frac { I } { j \omega } \right| = \left| \frac { \varphi _ { p } } { j \omega Z _ { m } } { \cal M } \right| .
$$

The calculations based on above equations for the MME composite cantilever were performed by adopting the following measured material parameters for PZT-5H: $d _ { 3 1 } = - 3 2 7 \mathrm { p C } / \mathrm { N }$ and $s _ { 1 1 } ^ { E } = 1 5 . 0 8 \times 1 0 ^ { - 1 2 } \mathrm { m } ^ { 2 } / \mathrm { N } .$

For compare, the theoretical calculation of $V _ { o }$ with respect to frequency and load resistance based on Eq. (1) is plotted in Fig. 4(b). Obviously, the calculated results also exhibit the trend of $V _ { o }$ with respect to frequency and load resistance revealed by the experimental data.

The focus is then placed on the generated electric power output $P _ { o }$ of the MME composite cantilever. The experimentally measured frequency-dependent $P _ { o }$ with different load resistances are shown in Fig. 5(a). It is obvious that the resonance peak of $P _ { o }$ shifts from the side of $f _ { r } ^ { s c }$ to the side of $f _ { r } ^ { o c }$ with increasing $R _ { L }$ as that of $V _ { o }$ do. However, it is hard to observe the trend of the peak value with respect to $R _ { L }$ . Thus, the values of $P _ { o }$ with respect to frequency and load resistance were theoretically calculated based on Eq. (1) and the relation of $P _ { o } = V _ { o } ^ { 2 } / 2 R _ { L }$ , as shown in Fig. 5(b). As can be seen, there are two peak power outputs with the same magnitude at $f _ { r } ^ { s c }$ and $f _ { r } ^ { o c }$ corresponding to their respective optimum load resistances. To verify the theoretical calculations experimentally, we compare in Figs. 6(a) and 6(b), respectively, the theoretically calculated and experimentally measured values of $P _ { o }$ versus load resistance with excitations at $f _ { r } ^ { s c }$ and $f _ { r } ^ { o c }$ . The theoretical curves in Fig. 6(a) predict a peak $P _ { o }$ of $1 4 . 0 3 \mu \mathrm { W }$ for the optimum load resistances of $1 4 . 1 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ and $1 9 9 . 5 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ ,respectively, at $f _ { r } ^ { s c }$ and $f _ { r } ^ { o c }$ . The experimental results in Fig. 6(b) exhibit $1 4 . 4 \mu \mathrm { W }$ for $1 5 \ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ at $f _ { r } ^ { s c }$ and $1 4 . 6 \mu \mathrm { W }$ for $1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ at $f _ { r } ^ { o c }$ . These load resistances are close to the optimum ones and their peak power output are in good agreement with the predicted ones. Figure 6(c) displays the plot of $P _ { o }$ versus $H _ { a c }$ for excitation at $f _ { r } ^ { o c }$ with $R _ { L } = 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { k } \Omega$ showing that $P _ { o }$ varies with $H _ { a c }$ by a square relation $( P _ { o } \propto H _ { a c } ^ { 2 } )$ as predicted. Taking into account the volume of the tip magnets, the overhang volume of the MME composite cantilever is $1 . 2 4 5 ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ .Therefore, the maximum power density of this configuration for resonance excitation is about $1 1 . 7 3 \mathrm { \ : } \dot { \mu } \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { O e } ^ { 2 } \mathrm { \ : c m } ^ { 3 }$ , which is one order of magnitude higher than that of the ME energy harvester reported in Ref. 11.

The inset is the schematic of the charging-discharge circuit for storing and releasing the electric power generated by the MME composite cantilever. The switch position "1" is for charging the storage capacitor $C _ { s t }$ and the switch position $^ { * } 2 ^ { * }$ is for lighting up the LEDs. The left and right images of the LEDs show the states before and after they were lit up, respectively.

Storing the electric power generated by the MME composite cantilever and making use of it are of great importance toward practical applications of the energy harvester. They are generally realized by using a charging-discharging circuit with two consecutive steps (as shown in Fig. 7).28 An electrolytic capacitor of $4 7 \mu \mathrm { F }$ was used as the energy storage element and connected in parallel with a full wave rectifying bridge such that it could be charged and its voltage finally reached $2 \mathrm { V }$ . Upon accomplishing charging the storage capacitor, the stored electric power was used to drive 6 commercial light-emitting diodes (LEDs) and the emitted light lasted $0 . 1 { - } 0 . 2 { \mathrm { s } }$ .

In summary, we investigate a MME composite cantilever of a piezoelectric bimorph and tip magnets for lowfrequency magnetic energy harvesting. The MME composite cantilever shows superior magnetic energy harvesting performance with the maximum power density of $\mathrm { 1 1 . 7 3 } \mu \mathrm { W } / \mathrm { O e } ^ { 2 } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$ for excitations at the short- and open-circuit resonance frequencies $( < 1 0 0 ~ \mathrm { H z } )$ with their respective optimum load resistances. The result is one order of magnitude higher than that of previously reported ME energy harvester. Moreover, the experimental results are in good agreement with the theoretical predictions based on the equivalent circuit model. The electric power generated by the MME composite cantilever was stored by a capacitor and used to light up 6 LEDs. The proposed prototype of the magnetic field energy harvester can be further optimized by effectively designing its geometric parameters and choosing piezoelectric materials with high piezoelectric parameters according to practical applications.
